patient.chief_complaint: Drooping eyelids, double vision, and difficulty chewing
patient.history_present_illness: A 67-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, COPD, and prostate cancer on active surveillance presented for evaluation of progressive bilateral ptosis, double vision, and difficulty chewing over 3 months. His wife first noticed his eyelids drooping approximately 3 months ago, initially intermittent and worse in the afternoons. He then developed horizontal diplopia when looking to the left, which was intermittent and positional. He began having difficulty chewing tough foods — he would tire out halfway through a meal and would need to rest his jaw. He has lost approximately 4 pounds over the past 2 months because he avoids foods that require prolonged chewing. He denies dysphagia with liquids but acknowledges occasional difficulty with large solid boluses. His voice has become softer and more nasal sounding after talking for more than 5 minutes, which his wife has noticed. He has no history of neck or back pain, no extremity weakness at rest, no falls, no bowel or bladder dysfunction. He was initially referred to ophthalmology who noted no structural eyelid pathology and no proptosis. He was then seen by his primary care physician who ordered brain MRI, which was reportedly normal. He was subsequently referred to the neurology clinic where examination revealed clear fatigability. His COPD is well-controlled on tiotropium with moderate exercise tolerance. The pulmonologist was concerned about overlapping respiratory muscle weakness potentially contributing to his reduced exercise capacity. He has not had any recent infections or antibiotic treatments. He denies weight loss beyond the 4 pounds from reduced food intake.

findings.significance: Peripheral neuropathy excluded; baseline CMAP amplitudes normal (LEMS excluded)

specialized_test.impression: Clearly abnormal repetitive nerve stimulation with 10-14% decremental CMAP responses at 3 Hz in deltoid, nasalis, and masseter muscles. Post-exercise brief facilitation followed by exhaustion at 3 minutes. Normal baseline CMAP amplitudes on NCS. Findings are consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular transmission. Single-fiber EMG recommended for highest sensitivity. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.impression: Markedly abnormal SFEMG orbicularis oculi. Mean MCD 72 µs (reference <34 µs) with 70% blocking rate. Increased jitter and blocking indicate severely impaired neuromuscular junction transmission. Findings are consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular transmission. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.proposed: Prednisone for immunosuppression in MG in patient with Type 2 DM on metformin (HbA1c 7.8%)
interactions: Prednisone + metformin: corticosteroids antagonize insulin secretion and cause hyperglycemia; metformin will be insufficient to control steroid-induced hyperglycemia
Prednisone worsening: expected glucose increase 40-80 mg/dL with moderate doses
contraindications: High-dose steroids as sole initial MG therapy without glucose monitoring plan is dangerous in T2DM
Consider initiating insulin for glycemic control during steroid therapy
warnings: Start prednisone at low dose (10-15 mg/day) and escalate slowly to minimize glycemic impact and avoid MG crisis
Intensify glucose monitoring — check BG before meals and at bedtime
Consider endocrinology consultation for steroid-diabetes management
alternatives: Azathioprine as steroid-sparing first-line to minimize steroid dose

output.proposed: Continue tiotropium (muscarinic antagonist) for COPD in patient starting pyridostigmine (cholinesterase inhibitor) for MG
interactions: Tiotropium (M3 antagonist inhaled) + pyridostigmine (AChE inhibitor): theoretical pharmacological antagonism — anticholinergic tiotropium may reduce efficacy of cholinergic pyridostigmine at NMJ
Clinical significance: tiotropium is inhaled with local pulmonary effects; pyridostigmine acts at NMJ; antagonism is primarily theoretical and minimal in clinical practice
warnings: Monitor MG symptom control after initiating pyridostigmine — if inadequate, consider whether tiotropium is contributing
Do NOT discontinue tiotropium (COPD management critical); continue both and titrate pyridostigmine to symptom control
If concerns persist, ipratropium can be substituted for tiotropium with shorter duration of anticholinergic effect
alternatives: Ipratropium (shorter-acting) as alternative bronchodilator if tiotropium-pyridostigmine interaction clinically significant
Optimize pyridostigmine dose to overcome any pharmacological antagonism

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Myasthenia gravis, generalized (MGFA Class IIb), AChR antibody-positive with thymoma, complicated by COPD and diabetes

differential.diagnosis: Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome from prostate cancer
differential.key_features: Prostate cancer rarely causes LEMS; anti-VGCC negative; no baseline CMAP reduction; no 50Hz increment; ocular symptoms prominent (LEMS usually spares ocular)
Paraneoplastic panel negative; thymoma is the relevant oncological finding; anti-titin positive
COPD explains some FVC reduction but not ptosis, diplopia, or jaw fatigue; EMG shows NMJ disorder not respiratory muscle myopathy

critical_actions: Anti-AChR antibody panel and anti-titin (thymoma screening)
CT chest — thymoma identified and requires thymectomy
Serial NIF monitoring — COPD + MG double jeopardy for respiratory failure
Intensify glucose monitoring if steroids started — HbA1c 7.8% at risk for severe hyperglycemia
Thoracic surgery consultation for thymectomy with COPD-adjusted surgical planning
Paraneoplastic workup given prostate cancer history (negative — reassuring)
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT start high-dose corticosteroids without glucose monitoring plan in T2DM
Do NOT discontinue tiotropium (COPD medication) — critical for bronchospasm prevention
Do NOT use aminoglycosides (penicillin allergy noted — avoid cephalosporins and ensure no aminoglycosides)
key_reasoning_points: Anti-titin positive in elderly male with MG is a strong predictor of thymoma — CT chest confirms anterior mediastinal mass
COPD and MG both reduce FVC — NIF is more specific for NMJ-related respiratory weakness than FVC alone
Masseter muscle involvement (jaw fatigue, chewing difficulty) is characteristic of bulbar MG and can be confirmed by RNS of masseter
Prostate cancer requires paraneoplastic evaluation (LEMS from VGCC antibodies) but workup is negative — thymoma is the relevant cancer
Diabetes (HbA1c 7.8%) critically affects treatment planning — steroids will worsen glycemia significantly

red_herrings.intended_effect: Clinician may pursue extensive paraneoplastic workup for prostate cancer as cause of neuromuscular symptoms, delaying MG diagnosis
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Paraneoplastic panel negative; anti-titin positive pointing to thymoma (anterior mediastinal mass confirmed on CT); prostate cancer is an incidental finding in this context
